newsitem.title: FRANCE: French voters may make Chirac lame-duck president.
newsitem.headline: French voters may make Chirac lame-duck president.

text.p: French voters elect a new parliament on Sunday and may force Gaullist President Jacques Chirac into tense "cohabitation" with a leftist prime minister.
The outcome was thrown wide open after the Socialist- Communist bloc scored an upset win a week ago in the first round of the election following a dull campaign.

Chirac, his presidency on the line after his gamble to call snap election appeared to backfire, hastily dropped unpopular Prime Minister Alain Juppe and offered voters the "dream ticket" of socially-conscious Philippe Seguin and free-marketeer Alain Madelin.
If the ruling centre-right coalition loses, Chirac will be forced into uneasy "cohabitation" or power-sharing with a government led by Socialist leader Lionel Jospin.
On the eve of polling, rugby fans watching France's Rugby Union championship final between Toulouse and Bourgoin got an insight into their country's possible political future.

Millions of television viewers saw Chirac sharing the VIP stand with the two men best-placed to become his next prime minister. But Jospin was banished to the far end of the front row while Seguin sat at the president's left.
In case voters had any doubts where Chirac's preferences lay, he invited Seguin to dinner at the Elysee presidential palace before they travelled together to the match, won 12-6 by Toulouse.
The 39-million-strong electorate was choosing 577 National Assembly deputies. Sunny weather was forecast for much of France with rain expected across the south.
Polling stations open at 8 a.m. (0600 GMT) in mainland France and close at 8 p.m. (1800 GMT). Television stations will broadcast projections of the result as soon as polls close.

Voters who abstained in the first round or who backed far right candidates appeared to hold the key to the result. Chirac's hopes depended on winning over a large slice of those who deserted the ruling centre-right coalition a week ago.

"The Seguin-Madelin ticket has come pretty late. It blurs the outlook because there has never been a change of leader (a reference to Juppe) between the two rounds of an election," said political commentator Pascal Perrineau.

"The results of the first round show that the centre-right does have some reserves in the contingent which abstained. But that won't be enough. It must capture a majority of those who abstained and an important slice of voters who backed the far-right National Front," Perrineau told France-Info radio.

National Front leader Jean-Marie Le Pen, whose party took 15 percent of the vote a week ago, urged voters to "punish" the ruling coalition, but centre-right leaders clearly sought to win some of those votes.
They appealed to voters to think of the future rather than venting short-term irritation at record unemployment and austerity measures needed to qualify France for a European single currency.
In the first round, when the combined left polled 40.1 percent of the vote to 36.5 for the centre-right, candidates were separated by less than two percentage points in 80 of the 577 constituencies.
